newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan assailed for treating stray dogs like trash.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan assailed for treating stray dogs like trash.

text.p: Despite its vast wealth, Taiwan treats its two million stray dogs like living trash, rounding them up for brutal executions or causing cruel deaths through neglect, animal rights activists said on Tuesday.

Taiwan's Life Conservationist Association and Britain's World Society for the Protection of Animals said in a report titled "Disposable Dogs: Made in Taiwan" that the island was "one of the worst places in the world to be a dog".
"The management and fate of stray dogs must be one of the worst, possibly the worst, situations in the world," it said.

Campaigners rallied in Taipei on Tuesday to condemn Taiwan for what the report called "systematic and appalling cruelty" to the thousands of stray dogs that are rounded up every year. They said 66,000 were captured in 1995 alone.

British, U.S., French and Australian activists assailed what they called Taiwan authorities' brutal treatment of captured dogs, saying they were electrocuted, drowned in cages, buried alive or simply left to starve in their cages.
Activists said they had visited 67 centres for holding stray dogs in November and December and found conditions unacceptable at 48 and poor at 12.

"The majority of dogs seen -- approximately 5,000 -- whether in old or new facilities were suffering with severe skin problems, were severely traumatised, with many close to death," the society's report said.
"Dead and decaying dogs were seen amongst the living, also dogs eating dogs. Humans at some of the sites seemed oblivious to the intense suffering around them."
Sociologists attribute the problem to people who buy or receive puppies as gifts, only to set them loose on the streets after discovering how much time and money having a pet demands.
For most citizens, putting a dog down is an unthinkable option in Taiwan, where Buddhist traditions are strong. As a result, most residential areas swarm with stray dogs.
Activists said a law to protect the rights of strays was stalled in parliament despite appeals in Taiwan and abroad.
Princess Elizabeth de Croy of France told Reuters that Taiwan's government appeared unconcerned.
"We hope Taiwan can get legislation of the animal protection law passed as soon as possible," she said in an interview.
She brought a message from Tibet's exiled spiritual leader the Dalai Lama calling for better treatment of stray dogs.

"I'm always distressed when animals are captured, caged and exploited for various human uses, thus causing tremendous suffering to these animals," Tibet's exiled god-king, who is scheduled to visit Taiwan in late March, said in the statement.
Dorothy Oliver of Humans, Environment and Animals Relating Together warned Taiwan "must act with the highest ethics and conscience" before it can be recognised as a developed country.
